brief.reader: People weighing whether a paid 30-day challenge is worth it
brief.problem: They suspect challenges are gimmicks with badges and hype
brief.outcome: They can judge any challenge by the three parts with real evidence behind them
brief.mainPoint: Game features alone add little; goals, tracking and choosing your own goal held up best
brief.structure: myth check with evidence, then a checklist to judge any challenge
brief.slide2Check: Hook2 reframes the yes/no question as 'badges do less, plain habits do more': same promise, new angle, works alone

slides.top: Points and badges do less than you'd think, and a few plain habits do more.

slides.text: extra steps a day: the average gain from game features in health apps across 36 trials. The researchers called it trivial.
In learning research, game features helped test scores. The boost to motivation held up less well in the strongest studies.

items: Choosing your own goal and starting now: 500 adults

chat.text: So what should a challenge have?
A clear goal, a deadline and a way to track it.

slides.text: Before you join any challenge, check for those three. Prizes and badges are the extra on top.
The $1K Challenge has all three. Comment CHALLENGE and I'll send you the details.

caption: Comment CHALLENGE and I'll send you the $1K Challenge page. It's $45 one time, with 30 days, your personal $1K Plan and a weekly check-in. Every study here measured health, learning or everyday behaviour, so none of them shows a challenge will earn you money. What they do show is which parts help people follow through, and those are the parts worth checking for before you sign up for anything.
